title: Commentariorum In Danielem Prophetam Liber Unus
author: Jerome
source: Translated by Claude from tmp465.tmp465.opp-lat1, as held by Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina.
statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.

passages.original: Ad intelligendas autem extremas partes Danielis, multiplex Graecorum historia ne- cessaria est : Sutorii videlicet 2 Callinici, Diodori, Hieronymi, Polybii, Posidonii, Claudii, Theonis, et Andronici cognomento Alipii, quos et porphyrius esse secutum se dicit : Josephi quoque et eorum quos ponit Josephus, praecipueque nostri Livii, et Pompeii Trogi, atque Justini, qui omnem (Al. omnes] extremae visionis narrant historiam, et post Alexandrum usque ad Caesarem Angustum, Syriae et AEgypti, id est, Seleuci, ct Antiochi, et Ptolemaeo- Tum bella describunt.
passages.english: To understand the last parts of Daniel, however, a wide range of Greek history is needed: namely that of Sutorius Callinicus, Diodorus, Hieronymus, Polybius, Posidonius, Claudius, Theon, and Andronicus surnamed Alipius, whom Porphyry too says he has followed; also of Josephus and of those whom Josephus cites, and especially of our own Livy, and of Pompeius Trogus and Justin, who narrate the whole history of the last vision, and describe, after Alexander down to Caesar Augustus, the wars of Syria and Egypt, that is, of Seleucus, Antiochus and the Ptolemies.
passages.notes: "Sutorii videlicet 2 Callinici": the '2' is a footnote mark; the name is usually read as Sutorius (or Suctorius) Callinicus, perhaps the sophist Callinicus of Petra. "Alipii" is perhaps for Alypius. A variant reads "omnes" for "omnem".

passages.original: Quod ita solvunt Hebraei, secun- dum hic annum dici regni ejus, omnium 627 gentium barbararum, non Judaeae tantum et Chal- daeorum, sed Assyriorum quoque et AEgyptiorum, et Moabitarum, et reliquarum nationum, quas, Domino concedente, superarat. Unde et Josephus in decimo Antiquitatum scribit libro : Post annum secundum AEgyptiae vastitatis, rex Nabuchodosor vidit mirabile somnium, et conterritus est spiritus ejus et somnium ejus fugit ab eo. Vidit rex impius somnium futurorum, ut interpretante sancto quod viderat, Deus glorificaretur;
passages.english: The Hebrews resolve this as follows: that here the second year of his reign is reckoned over all the barbarian nations, not only Judaea and the Chaldaeans, but also the Assyrians and Egyptians, and the Moabites, and the remaining nations which, by the Lord's permission, he had overcome. Hence Josephus too writes in the tenth book of the Antiquities: "After the second year of the devastation of Egypt, King Nebuchadnezzar saw a wondrous dream, and his spirit was terrified, and his dream fled from him." The impious king saw a dream of future things, so that, when a holy man interpreted what he had seen, God might be glorified;
passages.notes: The figure 627 is a page number from the printed edition and has been omitted.

passages.original: « Somnium tuum et visiones capitis tui in cu- bili tuo, hujuscemodi sunt. » Non dixit, visiones oculorum tuorum : ne quid putaremus esse corpo- reum, sed capitis : Sapientis enim oculi in capite ejus (Eccli.II, 14) : in principali videlicet cordis, juxta illud quod in Evangelio legimus : Beati mnndo corde, quoniam ipsi Deum videbunt (Matth. V, 8). Et : Quid cogitatis in cordibus vestris2 (Ibid. 4)? Alii vero ex hujus occasione capituli τ6 ήγεμο- νιχδν non in corde, sed juxta Platonem in cere- bro suspicantur.
passages.english: "Your dream and the visions of your head upon your bed are of this kind." He did not say "the visions of your eyes," lest we should think it something bodily, but "of your head": for "The wise man's eyes are in his head" (Eccles. 2:14), that is, in the ruling part of the heart, according to what we read in the Gospel: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matt. 5:8). And: "Why do you think [these things] in your hearts?" (ibid. 9:4). Others, however, taking occasion from this chapter, suppose that the *hēgemonikon* [ruling faculty of the soul] is not in the heart but, following Plato, in the brain.
passages.notes: The Greek is garbled by the scan (τ6 ήγεμονιχδν) and is read as τὸ ἡγεμονικόν. The reference "Eccli. II, 14" is actually to Ecclesiastes 2:14; "Ibid. 4" refers to Matt. 9:4.

passages.original: In fine autem horum omnium regnorum auri, argenti, airis el ferri, abscissus est lapis, Dominus atque Salvator, sine manibus, id est, absque coitu et humano semine, dc utero virginali, et contritis omnibus regnis, factus est mons magnus, et implevit universam terram : quod Judaei et impius Porphyrius male ad populum referunt Is- rael, quem in fine saeculorum volunt esse fortis- simum, et omnia regna conterere, et regnare in aetenum.
passages.english: At the end of all these kingdoms of gold, silver, bronze and iron, a stone was cut out, the Lord and Saviour, without hands, that is, without intercourse and human seed, from a virginal womb; and when all the kingdoms had been crushed, it became a great mountain and filled the whole earth. The Jews and the impious Porphyry wrongly refer this to the people of Israel, who they hold will at the end of the ages be the strongest, crush all kingdoms, and reign for ever.

passages.original: (Vers. 46.) « Et non cessabant qui miserant eos ministri regis succendere fornacem naphtha, et stupa. » Sallustius scribit in Historiis 1, quod naphtha sit genus fomitis apud Persas quo vel maxime nutriamur incendia. Alii ossa olivarum quae projiciuntur cum amurca arefacta, naphthan appellari putant : unde et Graece πυρίνη dicitur ab eo quod r,ΰρ, id est, ignem nutriat.
passages.english: (Verse 46.) "And the king's servants who had thrown them in did not cease to heat the furnace with naphtha and tow." Sallust writes in the Histories that naphtha is a kind of tinder among the Persians by which fires are especially fed. Others think that the stones of olives, which are thrown out with the dregs of the oil and dried, are called naphtha; hence in Greek too it is called *pyrinē*, because it feeds *pyr*, that is, fire.
passages.notes: "nutriamur" is evidently a misprint for "nutriantur" (are fed). The Greek ΰρ is read as πῦρ.

passages.original: Signa et mi- rabilia fecit apud me Deus excelsus : placuit ergo mihi praedicare ejus signa, quia magna sunt, ct mirabilia ejus, quia fortia, et regnum ejus, quia [Vulg. tacet quia] regnum sempiternum, et pote- stas ejus in generatione et generationem. » Epi- stola Nabuchodonosor in prophetae volumine po- nitur : ut non fictus ab alio postea liber sicut sycophanta (Porphyrius) mentitur, sed ipsius Da- nielis esse credatur.
passages.english: "The most high God has worked signs and wonders with me: so it has pleased me to proclaim his signs, because they are great, and his wonders, because they are mighty, and his kingdom, because [it is] an everlasting kingdom, and his power [is] from generation to generation." The letter of Nebuchadnezzar is placed in the prophet's book, so that the book may be believed to be Daniel's own, not forged later by someone else, as the slanderer (Porphyry) falsely claims.
passages.notes: The edition notes that the Vulgate omits the second "because".

passages.original: 1.) « Bahhasar rex ferit grande convivium optimatibus suis mille : et unu- quisque secundum suam bibebat aetatem. » Scien- dum est non hunc esse filium Nabuchodonosor, ut vulgo legentes arbitrantur; sed juxta Berosum 2, qui Chaldaeam scripsit historiam, et Josephum, qui Berosum sequitur, post Nabuchodonosor qui re- gnavit annis quadraginta tribus successisse in regnum ejus filium qui vocabatur Evilmarodach, de quo scribit Jeremias, quod in primo anno regni sui levaverit caput Joachin regis Judae, et eduxerit cum de domo carceris (Jerem. LII). Re- fert idem Josephus, quod post mortem Evilmaro- dach, in regnum patris successerit filius ejus Ne- glisar : post quem ·rursum filius ejus Labosor- dach 3 : quo mortuo Balthasar filius ejus regnum tenuerit, quem nunc Scriptura commemorat : quo interfecto a Dario rege Medorum, qui Cyri regis Persarum avunculus fuit, et Cyro Persa (quae duo regna Isaias (cap.XXI) ascensorem bigae, ca- meli, et asini vocat) destructum esse imperium Chaldaeorum. Quod quidem et Xenophon in Cyri majoris scribit infamia : et Pompeius Trogus, et multi alii qni barbaras scripsere historias. Hunc Darium in Graecis voluminibus quidam Astyagen [Al. Astyagea], alii Astyagis filium putant, et alio apud eos appellari nomine : Unusquisque autem principum vocatorum juxta suam bibebat aetatem;
passages.english: 1.) "King Belshazzar made a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and each drank according to his age." It should be known that this man was not the son of Nebuchadnezzar, as ordinary readers suppose; but according to Berossus, who wrote a history of Chaldaea, and Josephus, who follows Berossus, after Nebuchadnezzar, who reigned forty-three years, his son called Evil-merodach succeeded to his kingdom. Of him Jeremiah writes that in the first year of his reign he lifted up the head of Jehoiachin king of Judah and brought him out of the prison house (Jer. 52). The same Josephus reports that after the death of Evil-merodach his son Neglisar succeeded to his father's kingdom; after him in turn his son Labosordach; and when he died his son Belshazzar held the kingdom, whom Scripture now mentions. When he was killed by Darius king of the Medes, who was the maternal uncle of Cyrus king of the Persians, and by Cyrus the Persian (which two kingdoms Isaiah (ch. 21) calls the rider of the two-horse chariot, of the camel, and of the ass), the empire of the Chaldaeans was destroyed. Xenophon too writes this in the [Education] of the elder Cyrus, as do Pompeius Trogus and many others who wrote barbarian histories. This Darius some in Greek books think to be Astyages, others the son of Astyages, and called by another name among them. Each of the princes who had been invited drank according to his age;
passages.notes: "infamia" is evidently a corruption of "infantia" (i.e. the Cyropaedia, the Education of Cyrus); "Bahhasar" and "ferit" are scanning errors for Balthasar and fecit. The numbers 2 and 3 are footnote marks.

passages.original: « Regina autem, pro re quae acciderat regi et optimatibus ejus, domum convivii ingressa est, » etc. 654 Hanc Josephus aviam Balthasaris, Origenes matrem scribunt : unde et novit praeterita, quae rex ignorabat. Evigilet ergo Porphyrius qui eam Balthasaris somniatur uxorem, et illudit plus scire, quam maritum.
passages.english: "But the queen, because of what had happened to the king and his nobles, entered the banqueting house," etc. Josephus writes that she was Belshazzar's grandmother, Origen that she was his mother; hence she also knew past events of which the king was ignorant. So let Porphyry wake up, who dreams that she was Belshazzar's wife, and mocks [her] for knowing more than her husband.
passages.notes: The figure 654 is a page number. "illudit" may be a corrupt reading; the sense might be that Porphyry jeers at her knowing more than her husband.

passages.original: (Vers. 30.) « Eadem nocte interfectus est Bal- thasar rex Chaldaeus, et Darius Medus successit in regnum, annos natus sexaginta duos. » Josephus scribit in decimo Judaicae antiquitatis libro, ob- sessa Babylone a Medis et Persis, Dario videlicet et Cyro in tantam venisse Balthasar regem Baby- lonis oblivionem sui, ut celeberrimum iniret con- vivium, et in vasis templi biberet, et obsessus vacaret epulis.
passages.english: (Verse 30.) "That same night Belshazzar the Chaldaean king was killed, and Darius the Mede succeeded to the kingdom, being sixty-two years old." Josephus writes in the tenth book of the Jewish Antiquities that while Babylon was besieged by the Medes and Persians, namely Darius and Cyrus, Belshazzar king of Babylon came to such forgetfulness of himself that he held a most splendid banquet and drank from the vessels of the temple, and though besieged gave himself up to feasting.

passages.original: omne populi], tribus, et linguae ipsi servient. Potestas ejus, potestas aeter- na, quae non auferetur, et regnum ejus, quod non corrumpetur, » etc. Hoc cui potest hominum con- venire, respondeat Porphyrius : aut quis iste tam potens sit, qui cornu parvulum, quem Antiochum interpretatur, fregerit atque contriverit? Si respon- derit Antiochi principes, a Juda Machabaeo fuisse superatos, docere debet quomodo cum nubibus coeli veniat, quasi Filius hominis, et offeratur Ve- tusto dierum, et detur ei potestas, et regnum, et 671 omnes populi, tribus ac linguae serviant illi, et potestas ejus aeterna sit, quae nullo fine clauda- tur.
passages.english: [all peoples], tribes and tongues shall serve him. His power is an everlasting power, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom one that shall not be destroyed," etc. Let Porphyry answer to which of men this can apply; or who is this one so powerful that he broke and crushed the little horn, which he interprets as Antiochus? If he replies that the princes of Antiochus were overcome by Judas Maccabaeus, he must show how [Judas] comes with the clouds of heaven like a Son of Man, and is brought to the Ancient of Days, and power and a kingdom are given to him, and all peoples, tribes and tongues serve him, and his power is everlasting, closed by no end.
passages.notes: The figure 671 is a page number. The opening bracket belongs to a variant reading ("omne populi" for "omnes populi") that begins in the preceding context.

passages.original: » Pro chrysolitho 6, qui unus est de duode- cim lapidibus qui ponuntur in logio pontificis, in Hebraeo habet (OTKin) THARSIS, quod Theo- dotio et Symmachus eodem verbo interpretati sunt; Septuaginta vero mare appellaverunt, juxta illud quod in psalmo legimus : In spiritu violento confrin- ges naves Tharsis (Psal. XLVII, 8), id est, maris. Et donas fugere cupiebat non in Tharsum urbem Ciliciae, ut plerique aestimant, litteram ponentes pro littera, vel Indiae regionem, ut putat Josephus 7 sed absolute in pelagus (Jon.I).
passages.english: "For 'chrysolite', which is one of the twelve stones placed on the high priest's oracle-breastpiece, the Hebrew has THARSIS, which Theodotion and Symmachus rendered with the same word, while the Septuagint called it 'sea', in line with what we read in the psalm: 'With a violent wind you will shatter the ships of Tharsis' (Ps. 47:8), that is, of the sea. And Jonah wished to flee not to Tarsus, a city of Cilicia, as most suppose, putting one letter for another, nor to a region of India, as Josephus thinks, but simply out onto the open sea (Jonah 1).
passages.notes: The leading » and the stray numerals (6, 7) are editorial or footnote marks and are omitted. '(OTKin)' appears to be a garbled rendering of the Hebrew word and is left untranslated. 'donas' is read as 'Jonas' (Jonah). 'logio' refers to the oracle-breastpiece (logion) of the high priest.

passages.original: 20.) « Et stabit in loco ejus vilissimus, et indignus decore regio : et in paucis diebus coute- retur, non in furore, nec in praedio. » Seleucum dicit cognomento Philopatorem 711 filium Magni Antiochi, qui nihil dignum Syriae et patris gessit imperio, et absque ullis prodi is inglorius periit. Porro Porphyrius non vult hunc esse Seleucum, sed Ptolemaeum Epihanen, qui Seleuco sit molitus insidias, et adversum eum exercitum praepararit, et idcirco veneno sit interfectus a ducibus suis. Quod cum unus ab illo quaereret, tantas res moliens ubi haberet pecuniam?
passages.english: 20.) "And in his place there will stand one most contemptible and unworthy of royal honour; and in a few days he will be crushed, not in fury nor in battle." He means Seleucus, surnamed Philopator, son of Antiochus the Great, who did nothing worthy of the empire of Syria and of his father, and perished ingloriously without any battles. Porphyry, however, will not have this be Seleucus, but Ptolemy Epiphanes, who is supposed to have plotted against Seleucus and prepared an army against him, and for that reason to have been killed by poison by his own generals. For when one of them asked him, since he was undertaking such great enterprises, where he would get the money,
passages.notes: The opening '20.)' is the end of a verse reference (Dan. 11:20) begun in the preceding context. 'praedio' is read as 'praelio' (battle), and 'prodi is' as 'praeliis' (battles). '711' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted.

passages.original: Et rex Austri provocabitur ad bellum multis auxiliis, et fortibus nimis : et non stabunt, quia inibunt adversum eum consilia. Et comedentes pa- nem cum eo conterent eum : exercitusque ejus opprimetur, 714 et cadent interfecti plurimi. » Haec Porphyrius interpretatur de Antiocho, qui adversus Ptolemaeum sororis suae filium profectus est cum exercitu magno. Sed et rex Austri, id est, duces Ptolemaei provocati sunt ad bellum multis auxiliis, et fortibus nimis, et non potuerunt resi- stere Antiochi consiliis fraudulentis;
passages.english: And the king of the South will be provoked to war with many and very strong forces; and they will not stand, because plans will be laid against him. And those who eat bread with him will crush him; and his army will be overwhelmed, and very many will fall slain." Porphyry interprets this of Antiochus, who set out with a great army against Ptolemy, his sister's son. But the king of the South too, that is, Ptolemy's generals, were provoked to war with many and very strong forces, and could not withstand the deceitful plans of Antiochus;
passages.notes: '714' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted.

passages.original: Et rex Austri provocabitur ad bellum multis auxiliis, et fortibus nimis : et non stabunt, quia inibunt adversum eum consilia. Et comedentes pa- nem cum eo conterent eum : exercitusque ejus opprimetur, 714 et cadent interfecti plurimi. » Haec Porphyrius interpretatur de Antiocho, qui adversus Ptolemaeum sororis suae filium profectus est cum exercitu magno. Sed et rex Austri, id est, duces Ptolemaei provocati sunt ad bellum multis auxiliis, et fortibus nimis, et non potuerunt resi- stere Antiochi consiliis fraudulentis;
passages.english: And the king of the South will be provoked to war with many and very strong forces; and they will not stand, because plans will be laid against him. And those who eat bread with him will crush him; and his army will be overwhelmed, and very many will fall slain." Porphyry interprets this of Antiochus, who set out with a great army against Ptolemy, his sister's son. But the king of the South too, that is, Ptolemy's generals, were provoked to war with many and very strong forces, and could not withstand the deceitful plans of Antiochus;
passages.notes: This passage duplicates p17747. '714' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted.

passages.original: Porphyrius autem et exteri qui sequuntur sum, de Antiocho Epiphane dici arbitrantur quod erectus sit contra cultum Dei, et in tantam su- perbiam venerit, ut in templo Jerosolymis simu- lacrum suum poni jusserit. Quodque sequitur : Et diriget, donec compleatur ira, quia in ipso erit ron- summatio, sic intelligunt, tam diu eum posse, do- nec irascatur ei Deus, et ipsum interfici jubeat. Siquidem Polybius et Diodorus qui Bibliotheca- rum 3 scribunt historias, narrant eum non solum contra Deum fecisse Judaeae, sed avaritiae facibus accensum, etiam templum Dianae in Elimaide 1, quod erat ditissimum, spoliare conatum : oppres- sumque a custodibus templi vicinis circum genti- bus, et quibusdam phantasiis atque terroribus versum in amentiam, ac postremum morbo inter- iisse, et hoc ei accidisse commemorant, quia tem- plum Dei violare conatus sit.
passages.english: Porphyry, however, and the others who follow him, think it is said of Antiochus Epiphanes that he was raised up against the worship of God and came to such pride that he ordered his own image to be set up in the temple at Jerusalem. And what follows, 'And he will prosper until the wrath is completed, for in him will be the consummation', they understand thus: that he would have power just so long as God was not angry with him and did not order him to be killed. For indeed Polybius and Diodorus, who write the histories of the 'Libraries', relate that he not only acted against the God of Judaea, but, inflamed by the torches of greed, also tried to plunder the temple of Diana in Elymais, which was very rich; that he was overpowered by the guardians of the temple and the peoples living round about, and was driven to madness by certain apparitions and terrors, and at last died of disease; and they record that this befell him because he had tried to violate the temple of God.
passages.notes: 'exteri' is read as 'ceteri' and 'sum' as 'eum'. 'ron- summatio' is read as 'consummatio'. Stray numerals (3, 1) are footnote marks and are omitted. 'Bibliothecarum ... historias' presumably refers to Diodorus's Bibliotheca. 'contra Deum ... Judaeae' is read as 'against the God of Judaea'. The final clause seems to reflect Polybius's view that he was punished for trying to violate a temple (that of Diana). Jerome reinterprets it as the temple of God.

passages.original: Soli Septuaginta omni se no- minis quaestione liberantes interpretati sunt : Et statuet tabernaculum suum tunc inter maria, et montem voluntatis sanctum, et veniet hora consum- mationis ejus. Quos Apollinarius secutus, de nomi- ne Apedno omnino conticuit. Hoc ideo prolixius posui, ut et Porphyrii ostendam calumniam qui haec omnia ignoravit, aut nescire se finxit, et Scripturae sanctae difficultatem : cujus intelligen- tiam absque Dei gratia et doctrina majorum sibi imperitissimi vel maxime vindicant.
passages.english: Only the Seventy, freeing themselves from every question about the name, translated: 'And he will then set up his tent between the seas and the holy mountain of [his] will, and the hour of his consummation will come.' Apollinarius followed them and kept completely silent about the name Apedno. I have set this out at some length in order to show both the slander of Porphyry, who was ignorant of all this or pretended not to know it, and the difficulty of holy Scripture, the understanding of which the most unskilled claim for themselves above all, without the grace of God and the teaching of their elders.
passages.notes: 'Apedno' is the Hebrew place-name (Apadno/Aphedno), spelled 'Aphedano' in the preceding context. 'montem voluntatis sanctum' is ambiguous and may mean 'the holy mountain of delight'.

passages.original: Et hoc, inquit, de Antiocho scriptum est, qui vadens in Persidem, Lysiae qui Antiochiae, et Phoeniciae (Al. Phoenici) praeerat, reliquit exer- citum, at adversum Judaeos pugnaret, urbemque eorum Jerusalem subverteret; quae omnia narrat Josephus historiae auctor Hebraeae, quod talis fuerit tribulatio, qualis nunquam, et tempus advenerit quale non fuit ex quo gentes esse coe- perunt usque ad illud tempus. Reddita autem victoria, et caesis Antiochi ducibus, ipsoque An- tiocho in Perside mortuo, salvatus est populus Israel : omnes qui scripti erant in libro Dei, hoc est, qui legem fortissime defenderunt, et econtra- rio qui deleti sunt de libro, hoc est, qui praevari- catores exstiterunt legis, et Antiochi fuerunt partium.
passages.english: "And this too," he says, "was written of Antiochus, who, setting out for Persia, left an army to Lysias, who governed Antioch and Phoenicia, so that he might fight against the Jews and overthrow their city Jerusalem. Josephus, the author of the Hebrew history, relates all these things: that there was tribulation such as never was, and a time came such as had not been since nations began to exist until that time. But when victory was restored, Antiochus's generals slain, and Antiochus himself dead in Persia, the people of Israel was saved: all who were written in the book of God, that is, those who most bravely defended the Law; and, on the contrary, those who were blotted out of the book, that is, those who proved transgressors of the Law and were of Antiochus's party.
passages.notes: 'at' is read as 'ut'. The speaker is Porphyry. The sentence about those 'blotted out of the book' is elliptical and lacks a main verb in the Latin.

passages.original: 7.) « Et audivi virum qui indutus orat lineis, qui stabat super aquas fluminis, cum ele- vasset dexteram, et sinistram suam in coelum, et jurasset per viventem in 728 aeternum, quia in tempus, et tempora, et dimidium temporis. Tempus, et tempora, et dimidium temporis, tres et semis annos interpretatur Porphyrius, quod et nos juxta Scripturarum sanctarum idioma, non negamus. Nam et supra legimus, quod septem tempora transierint super Nabuchodonosor, id est, septem anni effe- rationis ejus, et in visione quatuor bestiarum scriptum est, leonis, et ursi pardi, et alterius be- stiae, cujus nomen tacetur, quae regnum significat.
passages.english: 7.) "And I heard the man who was clothed in linen, who stood above the waters of the river, when he had raised his right hand and his left to heaven and had sworn by him who lives for ever, that [it would be] for a time, and times, and half a time." 'A time, and times, and half a time' Porphyry interprets as three and a half years, which we too do not deny, according to the idiom of the holy Scriptures. For above also we read that seven times passed over Nebuchadnezzar, that is, the seven years of his wildness; and in the vision of the four beasts it is written, of the lion, and the bear, the leopard, and another beast whose name is not given, which signifies the kingdom
passages.notes: The opening '7.)' is the end of a verse reference (Dan. 12:7) begun in the preceding context. 'orat' is read as 'erat'. The final sentence breaks off and continues in the following context ('...of the Romans'). '728' is a page number from the printed edition and is omitted.

passages.original: cum] abla- tum fuerit juge sacrificium, et posita fuerit abomi- natio in desolationem, dies mille ducenti nona- ginta. » Hos mille ducentos nonaginta dies Porphy- rius in tempore Antiochi, et in desolatione templi dicit completos, quam el Josephus et Machabaeorum (ut diximus) liber, tribus tantum annis fuisse com- memorant. Ex quo perspicuum est tres istos, et semis, annos de Antichristi dici temporibus, qui tribus et sera is annis, hoc est mille ducentis nona- ginta diebus, sanctos persecuturus est, et postea corruiturus in monte inclyto et sancto.
passages.english: [when] the perpetual sacrifice has been taken away and the abomination set up for desolation, one thousand two hundred and ninety days." Porphyry says these one thousand two hundred and ninety days were fulfilled in the time of Antiochus and in the desolation of the temple, which both Josephus and the book of Maccabees (as we have said) record as lasting only three years. From this it is clear that these three and a half years are spoken of the times of Antichrist, who for three and a half years, that is, one thousand two hundred and ninety days, will persecute the saints, and afterwards will fall on the glorious and holy mountain.
passages.notes: The text opens with an editorial bracket ('[Vulg. cum]') and the word 'cum' (when) is translated. 'el' is read as 'et', and 'sera is' as 'semis'.
